title: A first-of-its-kind multi-model convection permitting ensemble for investigating convective phenomena over Europe and the Mediterranean
problem: Assessing future convective extremes is challenging because coarse models poorly represent convection, and single convection-permitting model experiments are not robust enough to capture the full range of uncertainty, necessitating a coordinated, multi-model ensemble approach.
method: This paper presents a multi-model ensemble of convection-permitting simulations, run in weather-like and climate modes, to investigate present and future convective processes and related extremes over Europe and the Mediterranean.
task: The task is to build and analyze a multi-model convection-permitting ensemble to investigate present and future convective processes and related extreme weather events over Europe and the Mediterranean.
innovation: This paper presents a first-of-its-kind multi-model convection permitting ensemble project for investigating convective phenomena over Europe, providing preliminary results from test cases that demonstrate the value of an ensemble-based approach for simulating high-impact weather events.

A recently launched project under the auspices of the World Climate Research Program’s (WCRP) Coordinated Regional Downscaling Experiments Flagship Pilot Studies program (CORDEX-FPS) is presented. This initiative aims to build first-of-its-kind ensemble climate experiments of convection permitting models to investigate present and future convective processes and related extremes over Europe and the Mediterranean.

According to the station observations collected during the field campaign (Ducrocq et al. 2014, http://hoc.sedoo.fr for HyMeX data- base) three regions were mainly affected by heavy precipitation. Two areas were in Southern France-referred to as CV1 and CV2 and indicating, respectively, the western and eastern parts of the Cévennes-Vivarais (CV) observation site during the HyMeX campaign (see Fig. 1 in Ducrocq et al. 2014).
The third affected area was Liguria-Tuscany one (LT, Fig. 1 in Ducrocq et al. 2014).

Case 2 (called AUSTRIA hereafter) is a convective orographic precipitation event with weak but persistent large-scale driving factors that was induced by the evolution of a shallow trough over the North Atlantic, from 22 to 25 June 2009. A cutoff low was isolated over Southern Europe, thus inducing persistent northeasterly flow over Austria, associated with unstable warm-moist air, impinging on the Alps.
This caused extreme rainfall along the northern flanks of the Alps due to orographic lifting.

Case 3 (called FOEHN hereafter) is a Foehn event that occurred on November 2014 Kramer et al. (2017). In this case the slow eastward evolution of a deep trough, associated with a mid-latitude cyclone over the North Atlantic induced persistent southerly flow over the Alps.
